source_text: OK; it's interesting that it all goes via the .olean files at present, furthermore that we can just load them all into memory and read them there, that's interesting too.  I'd assume that generating the Python types to match would be a good step towards reading Python as a later demo.  I.e. we could see if we could round-trip some expressions.

reply_text:
A round trip is a good test of whether the types are right. Every typed value must convert back to a Lean object that the kernel's own equality says is identical. Concretely: Lean `Expr` → typed Python → Lean `Expr`, then compare by `Expr` hash and `lean_expr_eqv`, over every constant in a module. Once that holds, "Python → Lean" is the same back half fed from Python source.

First, the export recipe for rebuilding the package with the new driver entry points:I'm still tracing how the last IR export, with the driver included, was produced, so I can rebuild the generated package with the new entry points. Checking the session transcript:The build was done by a Codex lane on 10-09. Extracting the shell commands it ran:The extended driver compiles. Next I'm adding a native `--layout` mode, so the Python results have a native reference, and checking it on `Expr`:Writing the typed layer now. It reads layouts from Lean, generates Python dataclasses from Lean's inductive declarations, and converts values in both directions.The export has finished (343,592 functions); the package build is next. Writing `typed.py`:`lean_name_mangle` isn't an export. I'll call Lean's own `Name.mangle` function directly:Only 4 constants match per module, so something systematic differs. Locating the first difference on one constant:A process-limit warning ("fork: retry") just came up. My new task scheduler gives each Lean task its own thread, so I'm checking whether threads are piling up:Thread counts are normal (1,281 system-wide), so the warning was transient, probably from the package build. Reading Lean's trivial-structure rule itself:My `pkill -f` matched its own shell; I've made this mistake before. Retrying with explicit PIDs:The typed2 build had already finished, and the driver edit never ran because the shell was killed first. Re-applying it:Native results look right: `KVMap`, `MVarId`, `Subtype` and `Fin` are trivial; `Expr` isn't. Starting the typed3 package build, and adding trivial-structure handling to the typed layer:Testing in the running session, with native Lean standing in for the two driver entries until typed3 is built:The mismatches are inside universe levels (`Level`): a `max u v` whose argument `param u_1` comes back as a different constructor. Testing `Level` conversion on its own:typed3 is built. Checking the generated Python for `Expr`, so the demo's printer uses the real field names:That exists. While the demo runs, I'm stopping the debug session and writing a slow regression test for the round trip. It skips unless the package has the new driver entry points.The debug session is stopped. My `pgrep -f` matched its own shell again (the third time this session), so from now on I'll use the `[l]ean_repl.py` bracket form. Checking that the demo run survived:Now the slow test, sharing the kernel tests' single Lean start:The demo is still running; it'll notify me when done. In the meantime, the fast suite with the new code:The fast suite passes. Waiting for the end-to-end demo to finish.
